“But,” I said, handing the slip back to him, “I understand no more than before. Even if all the jewels of Golconda were offered as a reward for solving this puzzle, I'm quite sure I couldn't win them.”

“And yet,” Legrand said, “solving it is much less difficult than a quick first look at those symbols might suggest. As anyone could guess, they form a cipher—a message written in code. But from what we know of Kidd, I couldn't imagine him inventing one of the more complicated codes. I decided at once that this was a simple one, although a sailor with little learning would think it completely impossible to read without the key.”

“And you really worked it out?”

“Easily. I've solved others ten thousand times more complicated. My circumstances and a natural turn of mind have made me interested in such puzzles. I rather doubt that human cleverness can invent a code which human cleverness, properly applied, cannot solve. In fact, once I had obtained a connected series of readable symbols, I hardly thought about how difficult it might be to discover their meaning.

“In this case—as in every case of secret writing—the first question is what language the message uses. The methods of solving it, especially with simpler ciphers, depend on the special features of that language and change accordingly. Usually the only option is to try each language the person solving it knows, starting with the most likely, until the right one is found. But here the signature removed all that difficulty. The joke on the name ‘Kidd’ makes sense only in English. Without that clue, I would have started by trying Spanish and French, since a pirate operating along the Spanish Main would most naturally have written a secret like this in one of those languages. As things stood, I assumed the coded message was in English.

“You'll notice that there are no spaces between the words. If there had been, the job would have been relatively easy. I would have begun by comparing and studying the shorter words. If a word of just one letter had appeared, as it very probably would—‘a’ or ‘I,’ for instance—I would have considered the solution certain. But since the words weren't separated, my first task was to find which letters occurred most often, as well as which appeared least often.

He also had to consider Sybil's parents, who were fairly old-fashioned and might object to the marriage if there were even a hint of scandal. Still, he felt sure that if he explained all the facts, they would be the first to appreciate his motives. He therefore had every reason to choose poison. It was safe, reliable, and quiet, and removed any need for distressing scenes, which, like most Englishmen, he deeply disliked.

He knew absolutely nothing about the science of poisons, however. Since the waiter seemed unable to find anything in the library except Ruff's Guide and Bailey's Magazine, he searched the shelves himself. Eventually he discovered a handsomely bound Pharmacopoeia and a copy of Erskine's Toxicology, edited by Sir Mathew Reid, President of the Royal College of Physicians. Sir Mathew was also one of the Buckingham's longest-standing members, having been elected in mistake for someone else. This mishap so infuriated the Committee that when the intended candidate appeared, they unanimously voted against him. Lord Arthur found the technical vocabulary in both books quite bewildering and was beginning to regret neglecting his classical studies at Oxford when, in Erskine's second volume, he came upon a fascinating, detailed account of aconitine's properties, written in reasonably clear English. It struck him as precisely the poison he needed. Its action was rapid—indeed, almost instantaneous—and entirely painless. Taken in a gelatin capsule, as Sir Mathew advised, it was not at all unpleasant to swallow. He therefore noted on his shirt cuff the quantity required for a fatal dose, returned the books to their shelves, and strolled up St. James's Street to the distinguished chemists Pestle and Humbey. Mr. Pestle, who always served aristocratic customers himself, was considerably startled by the order and murmured with great deference that a medical certificate was required. But Lord Arthur explained that he needed it for a large Norwegian mastiff he was obliged to dispose of: the animal was showing early symptoms of rabies and had already bitten the coachman twice on the calf. Mr. Pestle then declared himself entirely satisfied, praised Lord Arthur's remarkable knowledge of toxicology, and had the prescription prepared at once.

Lord Arthur placed the capsule in a lovely little silver sweet box he spotted in a Bond Street shop window, discarded Pestle and Hambey's unattractive pillbox, and immediately drove to Lady Clementina's.

He had, moreover, to consider Sybil's father and mother, who were somewhat old-fashioned, and might well oppose the marriage if anything resembling a scandal arose; though he was convinced that, once acquainted with all the circumstances, they would be the first to understand the motives by which he had been governed. Everything, then, favoured his choice of poison. It was safe, certain, and noiseless, and dispensed with the need for those painful scenes to which he, in common with most Englishmen, entertained a deep objection.

Of the science of poisons, nevertheless, he was entirely ignorant, and since the waiter appeared incapable of discovering anything in the library beyond Ruff's Guide and Bailey's Magazine, he searched the shelves for himself. At last he found a richly bound edition of the Pharmacopoeia and a volume of Erskine's Toxicology, edited by Sir Mathew Reid, President of the Royal College of Physicians and one of the Buckingham's oldest members. He had been elected under the impression that he was somebody else—a contretemps which so angered the Committee that, when the proper gentleman presented himself, they unanimously black-balled him. Lord Arthur was considerably perplexed by the technical expressions in both works, and was beginning to wish he had attended more closely to his classics at Oxford, when the second volume of Erskine supplied a most interesting and thorough description of the properties of aconitine in tolerably plain English. Here, he thought, was the very poison he required. Its effect was swift—almost instantaneous, indeed—wholly painless, and, administered in a gelatine capsule, the method Sir Mathew recommended, it was by no means disagreeable to the taste. Accordingly, he wrote upon his shirt-cuff the quantity needed for a fatal dose, restored the books to their places, and sauntered up St. James's Street to the eminent chemists, Pestle and Humbey's. Mr. Pestle, who invariably served the aristocracy in person, was much astonished by his order, and murmured, with the greatest respect, something concerning the necessity of a medical certificate. Once Lord Arthur explained, however, that it was intended for a large Norwegian mastiff which he was compelled to destroy, as it exhibited the first signs of rabies and had twice bitten the coachman in the calf, he professed himself completely satisfied, congratulated Lord Arthur upon his admirable knowledge of Toxicology, and ordered the prescription to be made up without delay.

Lord Arthur transferred the capsule to a charming little silver bonbonnière he noticed in a Bond Street shop-window, discarded Pestle and Hambey's hideous pill-box, and drove straight to Lady Clementina's.
